items.headline: AI Agents Are Becoming the Web's Second Audience
items.background: Web design and information architecture have always assumed a human end-user. The rapid deployment of AI agents that autonomously browse, scrape, and act on the web is forcing a rethink of that foundational assumption.
keyFindings: Web content is increasingly consumed by AI agents, not just humans, requiring dual-audience design thinking
Structured, semantic markup that was previously an accessibility best practice now also improves AI agent parseability
Designing only for human visual experience may cause content to be misread or ignored by automated agents acting on users' behalf
items.implications: Product and content teams should audit whether their information architecture and markup is machine-readable, not just visually clear. This is most urgent for teams building content-heavy sites, APIs, or anything likely to be indexed or acted on by AI pipelines.

items.headline: Screen-Centric Design Is Losing Its Monopoly
items.background: Voice interfaces, spatial computing, wearables, and ambient computing are forcing designers to confront a discipline that has been almost entirely organized around the rectangle of a screen.
keyFindings: The assumption that a screen is the primary interface container is breaking down across voice, AR, and ambient device categories
Design systems and component libraries built for pixel grids do not transfer cleanly to spatial or audio-first contexts
Interface design may need to shift from visual composition toward interaction logic that is medium-agnostic
items.implications: Practitioners invested heavily in screen-based design systems should begin stress-testing their work against non-screen contexts. This is especially relevant for teams at companies with any roadmap exposure to voice, AR, or wearable surfaces.

items.headline: What Separates Useful Design Feedback from Noise
items.background: Design critiques are a standard part of product team workflows, but poorly structured feedback is a persistent source of wasted time and designer frustration, often reflecting opinion rather than grounded evaluation.
keyFindings: Effective critique separates observation, interpretation, and recommendation into distinct steps rather than collapsing them into a single judgment
Feedback anchored to specific user goals or design principles is more actionable than aesthetic preference
Common failure modes include prescribing solutions before diagnosing problems and critiquing execution when the brief itself is flawed
items.implications: Leads and PMs running crits should establish a shared vocabulary for what constitutes a complete critique statement. Teams without a structured format tend to default to preference-based feedback that designers cannot act on.

items.headline: NLnet Launches €6M Fund for Open Geospatial Tools
items.background: Open-source geospatial infrastructure is underfunded relative to its use in public-interest applications. NLnet Foundation, which funds internet freedom and open infrastructure projects, is directing significant capital into this gap.
keyFindings: NLnet Foundation is coordinating a €6 million GeoCommons fund targeting open geospatial software and infrastructure
The fund is positioned within the broader open-source sustainability funding landscape, where geographic and mapping tools have historically received less support than other OSS categories
GeoCommons-style infrastructure underpins civic tech, humanitarian mapping, and location-aware product features
items.implications: Product teams building on open geospatial stacks — or considering it — should watch this fund for projects that may mature or gain maintenance support as a result. Relevant for civic tech, urban planning tools, and any product with mapping dependencies.

items.headline: Dogfooding Catches Bugs — It Cannot Replace User Research
items.background: Internal product testing, or dogfooding, is widely used by tech teams as a quality signal. There is ongoing confusion about where dogfooding ends and where user research must begin.
keyFindings: Dogfooding surfaces implementation bugs and workflow gaps but introduces expert-user bias that makes it a poor proxy for real user behavior
Team members who built or deeply know a product cannot replicate the mental models, confusion points, or task contexts of first-time or low-context users
The three methods — dogfooding, QA, and user research — test for categorically different things and are not substitutable for each other
items.implications: Teams that rely on dogfooding as their primary validation method are likely shipping products that work for experts but fail for typical users. Dogfooding should be scoped strictly to bug and regression catching, with user research covering behavioral and comprehension questions.

items.headline: A Framework for Deciding Whether to Keep an AI Tool
items.background: Teams are under pressure to adopt AI tools without clear criteria for evaluating whether those tools actually improve outcomes. This has led to widespread adoption of tools whose value is assumed rather than demonstrated.
keyFindings: The PROVE framework isolates one specific task and one specific tool for evaluation, producing a structured provisional decision rather than a general impression
Pressure to adopt AI is explicitly named as a bias to control for — adoption pressure is not evidence of tool effectiveness
The framework produces a defensible, revisable decision, acknowledging that AI tool performance changes as models and interfaces update
items.implications: Product and design teams being asked to integrate AI tools into workflows should use a task-specific evaluation protocol before committing. The PROVE framework is particularly useful for making the case to stakeholders when declining to adopt a tool.
